ORIGINAL ARTICLE
Effect of micro‑oxygen pretreatment on gas production characteristics 
of anaerobic digestion of kitchen waste
Xiaofei Zhen1 · Xiaoyan Zhang1 · Shuaibing Li1 · Mingche Li1 · Jian Kang2
Received: 9 January 2020 / Accepted: 3 June 2020 / Published online: 15 June 2020 
© Springer Japan KK, part of Springer Nature 2020
Abstract
Micro-oxygen pretreatment of kitchen waste was done to improve the gas production efficiency of anaerobic fermentation 
and shorten the fermentation cycle of kitchen waste. The results demonstrated that with an oxygen supply of 20 mL, the peak 
gas production increased from 498 to 601 mL, and the theoretical gas production increased by 4.5 mL/g VS (volatiles solid) 
compared with those of the control group R1–R4. The anaerobic fermentation entered the late stage on day 25, which was 
13 days earlier than that of the control group. The chemical oxygen demand and ammonia nitrogen contents in the treatment 
groups of R1–R4 were relatively stable. An oxygen supply of 20 mL was conducive to stimulating the facultative anaerobes, 
promoting the decomposition of nitrogenous compounds and organic matter, and improving the anaerobic fermentation effi-
ciency. A lesser amount of oxygen (≤ 15 mL) was unable to effectively improve the gas production efficiency of anaerobic 
fermentation, although it exerted a certain inhibitory effect on anaerobic fermentation.
Keywords  Micro-oxygen pretreatment · Kitchen waste · Gas production characteristics · Anaerobic digestion
Introduction
With the continuous improvement in people’s living stand-
ards in China, the output of kitchen waste has also gradually 
increased. Kitchen waste has brought serious environmental 
pollution issues and a huge waste of resources. As a utiliz-
able resource with rich organic matter (OM), kitchen waste 
is gaining more and more attention [1, 2]. Anaerobic fermen-
tation is an approach to achieve reuse, reduce and recycle. 
The reaction is mainly divided into three stages, namely the 
hydrolytic acidification stage, the hydrogen production ace-
tic acid stage, and the methanogenesis stage. In the hydro-
lytic acidification stage OM is converted into small mol-
ecule organic matter by microorganisms. The small molecule 
organic matter is then converted into volatile fatty acids by 
the hydrogen-producing and acetic acid-producing groups 
of bacteria, and finally ­CH4 is produced by the methano-
gens using the volatile fatty acids. Anaerobic fermentation of 
kitchen waste, can not only reduce the OM content in kitchen 
waste, but also produce methane as a clean energy source. In 
addition, the produced biogas residue can also be used as a 
fertilizer, truly turning kitchen waste into a biomass resource 
[3, 4]. However, a major shortcoming is a long initial stage 
of the kitchen waste anaerobic fermentation. Thus, carry-
ing out efficient anaerobic digestion for kitchen waste has 
become a major concern of researchers.
In the progress in research on organic matter anaerobic 
digestion pretreatment has attracted increasing attention in 
the last decade. Studies have shown that the commonly used 
pretreatment methods for anaerobic digestion of organic 
matters mainly include mechanical (ultrasonic [5, 6], micro-
wave [7], electromagnetic high pressure homogenization

[8], etc.) pretreatment, thermal pretreatment [9], chemical 
(acid [10], alkali [11], ozone [12], Fenton [13], ­Fe2+ ion-
activated persulfate oxidation [14, 15]) pretreatment, and 
biological (fungi [16], enzymes [17], etc.) pretreatment.The 
pretreatment for anaerobic digestion of kitchen waste mainly 
aims to improve its rate of hydrolysis [18]. Araz Sedqi, et al. 
conducted aerobic pretreatment of the kitchen waste with 
four minerals (bentonite, fly ash, lightly burned MgO, and 
dolomite powder) for 4 h, and discovered that the alkaline 
minerals could adjust pH and enhance the capacity of ion 
exchange adsorption, thereby promoting the anaerobic fer-
mentation of kitchen waste [19]. Zhang et al. pretreated the 
kitchen waste with ultrasound to boost the yield of volatile 
fatty acids (VFAs), and found a 27.2% increase in their yield 
from kitchen waste after sonication [20]. Further, the deg-
radation efficiency could be enhanced by homogenizing the 
solid waste or increasing the specific surface area of solid 
particles to make it conducive to improving heat and mass 
transfer of the matrix [21, 22]. Li et al. found that thermal 
pretreatment reduced the oil potential, increased the stagna-
tion period of proteins and oils, but increased the cumula-
tive methane production. However, these pretreatments still 
have the problem of insufficient utilization of matrix [9]. 
The combined fermentation process of producing ethanol 
and methane from kitchen waste can overcome the problem 
of insufficient utilization of matrix and improve the energy 
recovery of the subsequent methane fermentation system. Li 
et al. compared the performance of micro-aerobic and anaer-
obic fermentation with corn stalk as substrate, and found that 
micro-aerobic conditions have strong buffer capacity and 
can tolerate the accumulation of large volatile fatty acids 
[23]. Martı´nez-Valdez et al. studied the mixing effect of 
aerobic pretreated organic fraction of municipal solid waste 
(OFMSW) and untreated OFMSW in the process of anaero-
bic digestion, and found that adding OFMSW after 5 days of 
pretreatment to untreated OFMSW could increase methane 
production by 18%, and that there was no significant dif-
ference in the lag time of methanogenic phase [24]. The 
effects of aerobic pretreatment and adding fly ash on meth-
ane production of mixed sludge were studied by Huilinir 
and Montalvo [25, 26], who found that the combined use 
of aerobic pretreatment and fly ash could increase methane 
production by more than 70%. Subsequently, Rafieenia et al. 
carried out anaerobic digestion of three substrates rich in 
carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids after aerobic pretreat-
ment, respectively, and observed that aerobic pretreatment 
could be used to improve substrate conversion efficiency 
and ­CH4 production in two-stage anaerobic digestion pro-
cess [27]. In this study, we explored the effect of the micro-
oxygen environment on the gas production characteristics 
of kitchen waste to improve the gas production efficiency 
during anaerobic digestion. By adding different amounts of 
oxygen to different experimental groups, we analyzed the 
changes in various parameters during the fermentation pro-
cess, studied the influence mechanism on each parameter, 
and tried to improve the fermentation efficiency. This study 
provides theoretical guidance for a practical set up of anaero-
bic fermentation of kitchen waste.
Materials and methods
Experimental materials
The kitchen waste used in this study was obtained from the 
Southern District Food Court of Shenyang Aerospace Uni-
versity. The hard-to-decompose materials such as eggshells, 
bones, and bags, etc. were removed because they cannot 
be anaerobically fermented. The inoculated sludge was 
obtained from the concentrated pool of the sewage treatment 
plant in northern Shenyang and was domesticated for 48 h 
after retrieving. The properties of the kitchen waste and the 
inoculated sludge are mentioned in Table 1.
Experimental methods
The sequencing batch reactor (SBR) for anaerobic fermenta-
tion comprised five units: a temperature controller, a reaction 
tank, a gas collecting unit, a drainage collecting unit and a 
connecting unit (Fig. 1). All units were connected to form a 
through-type closed equipment, where the reaction tank, the 
gas collecting unit, and the drainage collecting unit, 20 cm 
in height and all had an effective volume of 1 L. The entire 
small anaerobic fermentation bioreactor was strictly con-
trolled and airtight to ensure an anaerobic environment. At 
the start of the experiment, 100 g kitchen waste and 300 g 
inoculated sludge was added, and the volume was set to 1 
L with deionized water. A total of five experimental groups 
was set up. In the treatment groups R1–R4, oxygen at 5 mL, 
10 mL, 15 mL, and 20 mL was supplied respectively, and 
the group R5 was set as the blank control with no external 
oxygen supply. The experimental temperature was set at 
37 °C. The variation patterns of primary parameters such as 
daily gas production, cumulative gas production, pH, COD, 
and ammonia nitrogen were evaluated. The detection meth-
ods, instrument models, and measurement accuracy of these 
parameters are shown in Table 2.

Results and discussion
Effect of oxygen concentration on the characteristics 
of gas production
The variations in daily and cumulative methane yields of 
the anaerobic digestion of kitchen waste at varying concen-
trations of micro-oxygen a period of for 50 days are shown 
in Figs. 2, 3. All treated and control groups exhibited low 
methane yields initially. This was because, at the early stage 
of fermentation, the microbes in the inoculated sludge were 
still in the adaptation phase, and the hydrolytic fermenting 
microbes were the ones working primarily [28]. The theoret-
ical gas production can be obtained as the ratio of daily gas 
production to the VS content of the raw material. With the 
decomposition of organic macromolecules and the improved 
activity of methanogens, the groups R1–R4 reached the 
peak of first methane production at around day 10, Methane 
concentrations were 59.00%, 62.00%, 58.00%, 59.00%, and 
60.00%, and the calculated theoretical methane yields were 
15.43 mL/gVS(5 mL),15.56 mL/gVS(10 mL),18.03 mL/
gVS(15 mL) and 18.00 mL/gVS(20 mL). Whereas the con-
trol group reached the first gas peak yield on day 14, with 
a theoretical methane yield of 25.50 mL/gVS. As time pro-
gressed, the methane yield exhibited varying patterns with 
respect to various micro-oxygen concentrations. As shown 
in Fig. 2, the rise in methane yields of R1–R4 was faster 
with higher peak values than that in the control group R5, 
indicating improved gas production efficiency of the entire 
fermentation cycle. The treatment groups R1–R4 entered 
the late stage of the experiment by the 25th day. Around this 
time, the daily gas production was in a declining stage and 
the hydraulic retention time reached 25 days. This indicates 
the decomposition of most of the organic matter in the reac-
tion process is decomposed and the gas production starts to 
decline, while the control group R5 had a longer fermenta-
tion cycle and entered the late fermentation stage only on

day 38. In inter-group comparisons of R1–R4, it was found 
that with the increase in oxygen supply, and the peak value 
of methane yield gradually increased, along with a gradual 
improvement in the efficiency of anaerobic fermentation. 
Nevertheless, the treatment groups were unstable during 
the peak gas production stage, probably due to an unstable 
oxygen supply. Feng et al. [29] demonstrated that the micro-
oxygen amount could optimize the anaerobic fermentation 
system and increase the rate of fermentation by controlling 
the oxygen content under the initial conditions of anaerobic 
digestion of kitchen waste. Cumulative methanogenesis is 
consistent with the modified first-order hydrolysis model and 
the modified Gompertz model. This study uses a modified 
Gompertz model to fit the cumulative gas production. The 
fitting curve is shown in Fig. 3. The R1–R5 fitting curves R2 
are all above 0.99. The fitting effect is good. It can be seen 
that the modified Gompertz model can reflect the change 
of the cumulative gas production of anaerobic fermenta-
tion. The trends of cumulative methane yield for all groups 
was similar (Fig. 3), among which the curves of R3 (15 mL 
oxygen) and R4 (20 mL oxygen) exhibited with the high-
est slopes and superior gas production efficiencies. As the 
hydrolysis and acidification stage is the rate-limiting stage 
of anaerobic digestion, in the early hydrolysis stage of the 
anaerobic digestion, the addition of trace oxygen promotes 
the increase in numbers of facultative anaerobic bacteria 
such as yeast and Escherichia coli and is beneficial to the 
hydrolysis of macromolecular organic matter, Among the 
five groups, the highest cumulative methane yield was 
observed in R5. The final cumulative methane yields of 
R1–R5 were respectively 354.51 mL/gVS, 350.96 mL/gVS, 
381.56 mL/gVS, 399.25 mL/gVS, 398.44 mL/gVS. The 
above results indicate that the introduction of trace oxygen 
can shorten the reaction cycle of the hydrolysis stage of the 
anaerobic fermentation, improve the high anaerobic fermen-
tation treatment efficiency of the hydrolysis and acidification 
stage, and shorten the reaction cycle of anaerobic fermenta-
tion. Further, with the increase in the amount of oxygen, 
there is a gradual increase in efficiency.
Effect of oxygen concentration on pH of the reaction 
system
The variation in the pH of each group at different oxygen 
concentrations is shown in Fig. 4. In the initial stage, the 
anaerobic fermentation underwent hydrolysis/acidification. 
During this stage, the decomposition of organic macromol-
ecules like proteins and fats occurred in the reaction tank 
to form small organic molecules like fatty acids, producing 
a large amount of free ­H+, which led to drop in pH in the 
reaction tank [30–32]. As the fermentation progressed, the 
methanogens gradually adapted to the environment in the 
tank and began to use the free ­H+ in the system to syn-
thesize methane and ­CO2, resulting in an increase in pH 
of the system. On comparing the groups, R2 presented a 
pH significantly lower than that of the other groups during 
the enrire process, indicating a low efficiency of ­H+ utiliza-
tion by methanogens under such an oxygen concentration 
(10 mL). In the next stage, the pH of all groups increased 
sharply, indicating the depletion of free ­H+ by methanogens 
in the reaction system. However, at this stage the rate of 
increase in pH was not much different across the groups. 
The above results demonstrate that the micro-oxygen envi-
ronment may improve the efficiency of ­H+ utilization by 
methanogens, promote the activity of facultative anaerobes,

Effect of oxygen concentration on ammonia 
nitrogen content in the reaction system
In anaerobic fermentation, ammonia nitrogen exists pri-
marily in the forms of free ammonia ­(NH3) and ammonium 
cation ­(NH4
+). During the anaerobic fermentation, favorable 
ammonia nitrogen could be used as a nutrient to provide 
energy for the growth of microbes. However, the physiologi-
cal activity of methanogens is inhibited by excessively high 
ammonia nitrogen, resulting in ammonia inhibition [33, 34]. 
The variation of ammonia nitrogen during the fermentation 
at different oxygen concentrations is shown in Fig. 5. In the 
initial stages of fermentation, the ammonia nitrogen content 
was low in all the groups. As the fermentation proceeded, the 
rate of ammonia nitrogen produced by hydrolysis was much 
higher than its consumption in the reaction system, causing 
significantly elevated ammonia nitrogen content in all the 
groups (R1–R5). The ammonia nitrogen contents of R1–R5 
increased to 464 ± 26 mg/L, 462 ± 17 mg/L, 471 ± 32 mg/L, 
483 ± 23 mg/L, and 465 ± 14 mg/L, respectively, all of which 
stabilized around day 5. During the stable stage from day 5 
to day 30, the content of ammonia nitrogen was only slightly 
higher in the R4 group than in R1–R3 groups and was not 
significantly different among R1–R4. In uninduced ammonia 
nitrogen inhibition, higher ammonia nitrogen could provide 
abundant raw materials for microbial growth and metabo-
lism, allowing methanogens to utilize more small organic 
molecules, thereby enhancing the methane yield [35, 36]. In 
the later stage of fermentation, most of OM was exhausted, 
resulting in a higher rate of ammonia nitrogen consumption 
than production; hence, the ammonia nitrogen concentration 
decreased. Studies have shown that the addition of differ-
ent amounts of oxygen does not affect the performance of 
anaerobic digestion, but can improve the efficiency of desul-
furization in anaerobic fermentation and increase the redox 
potential of the system [37, 38]. Therefore, it can be inferred 
that during the anaerobic fermentation of kitchen waste, the 
ammonia nitrogen content of the micro-oxygen pretreatment 
groups was higher than that of the untreated control group, 
and that it increased with the increase in oxygen supply. 
The above results showed that the facultative anaerobes 
improved their capacity to produce and utilize nitrogenous 
compounds. Furthermore, increasing oxygen content pro-
moted the activities of facultative anaerobes in the system 
and enhanced the decomposition of organic macromolecules 
during fermentation.
Effect of oxygen concentration on COD content 
in the reaction system
The changes in COD directly represented the OM changes 
in the anaerobic fermentation system [39] (Fig. 6). In 
the initial stage of microbial adaptation, the degrada-
tion rate of small organic molecules was lower than that 
of larger ones, leading to a rise in cumulative COD in 
R1–R5. As the fermentation proceeded, the COD values 
of R1–R5 peaked on days 6–10, at 20,720 ± 220 mg/L, 
31,110 ± 670 mg/L, 24,167 ± 390 mg/L, 34,410 ± 510 mg/L, 
and 26,820 ± 530 mg/L, respectively. The peak COD indi-
cates the time when the microbes were the most active. The 
peak value and the time required to reach it may be used as a 
reference to determine the fermentation cycle. When the rate 
of microbial degradation of small organic molecules is faster 
than that of larger organic macromolecules, methanogens 
initiate the decomposition of substantially small organic

molecules such as VFAs which lead to an increase in gas 
production, consistent with our earlier analysis. Therefore, 
the content of small organic molecules decreased, followed 
by a decrease in the COD. In terms of the overall COD, 
the micro-oxygen pretreatment with an appropriate oxygen 
concentration could promote the anaerobic fermentation 
progress. The inhibition of anaerobes by a small amount of 
oxygen was more robust than the promotion of facultative 
anaerobes, causing the decline in overall hydrolytic effi-
ciency of the system. Feng et al. investigated the mechanism 
of micro-oxygen pretreatment on anaerobic fermentation. 
The results show that with the addition of ­O2, the cumulative 
gas production, COD and other parameters are improved. It 
is indicated that micro-oxygen activates aerobic and faculta-
tive anaerobic microorganisms in the system and promotes 
its participation in the hydrolysis and acidification process 
of macromolecular organic matter [40]; Other studies have 
shown that the addition of ­O2 can stimulate the chemical 
corrosion of sulfur-oxidizing bacteria and iron to induce 
microbial oxidation of sulfides to improve the methanogenic 
efficiency and control the ­H2S concentration in biogas [41]. 
After comparison it was observed that R4 (with 20 mL oxy-
gen supply) had the highest peak value, and it reached the 
peak the earliest, thus demonstrating that, without interfer-
ing with the anaerobic environment, oxygen supply of 20 mL 
could boost the activities of facultative anaerobes, enhance 
the decomposition of OM, improve the gas production effi-
ciency of anaerobic fermentation, and shorten the duration 
of the anaerobic fermentation cycle. In the present study, 
optimal hydrolysis and gas production was observed in the 
R4 (20 mL oxygen supply) system.
Conclusions
The daily methane yield displayed different patterns at dif-
ferent concentrations of oxygen in the anaerobic fermenta-
tion of kitchen waste. From the gas peak value and the time 
required to reach the peak, it can be inferred that at oxygen 
supply lower than 15 mL which is 0.83 mL/(gVS∙d), the 
inhibitory effect on anaerobes was far stronger than the pro-
motive effect on facultative anaerobes. The system exhibited 
significantly reduced gas production during the entire later 
stage of fermentation. The treatment group R4 exhibited the 
highest gas production with a cumulative methane yield of 
399.25 mL/gVS, and reached the peak the earliest, thereby 
shortening the duration of the anaerobic fermentation cycle.
Compared to the control group R5, groups with differ-
ent micro-oxygen concentrations demonstrated varying 
COD. The treatment group R4 with 20 mL oxygen supply 
presented the highest ammonia nitrogen and COD dur-
ing the digestion, with an ammonia nitrogen content of 
approximately 500 mg/L and a stable peak COD value of 
34410 ± 510 mg/L. The results demonstrated that an oxygen 
supply of 20 mL, which is 1.11 mL/(gVS∙d) could promote 
microbial utilization and decomposition of nitrogenous mol-
ecules, as well as other small organic molecules, improving 
the efficiency of anaerobic fermentation.
